184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes: The Office, in both its British original and its long-running American remake, is a mockumentary sitcom about the crushing banality of white-collar work, famous for cringe comedy and characters like the oblivious manager Michael Scott. This book argues the show earns serious treatment: its small workplace moments become tests of moral perception, self-deception, office romance, humor as a virtue, and whether weakness of will, not just malice, explains why ordinary people behave badly.
185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy: Saturday Night Live is NBC's late-night sketch comedy institution, running since 1975 and famous for political impressions, Weekend Update, and generations of comic catchphrases. A book of philosophy fits because sketch comedy keeps colliding with real questions: whom jokes may mock, whether offensive comedy can be social critique, how satire shapes political belief, and why parody sometimes lands as philosophy's own tool of unmasking rather than mere silliness.
186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The We: Spider-Man is Marvel's web-slinging superhero, the teenage Peter Parker whose motto that great power brings great responsibility is one of comics' most famous lines. His stories are unusually personal for a superhero: Uncle Ben's death, endless guilt, a double life, and constant choices between duty and happiness. That makes him a natural case study in the good life, infinite moral debt, obligation, forgiveness, and whether heroes actually get to live well.
187 - Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - B: Sons of Anarchy is FX's dark crime drama (2008-2014) about an outlaw motorcycle club in California, following Jax Teller's struggle between family, brotherhood, and the club's violent gun-running trade. The show's moral weight invites philosophy: viewers root for criminals, so the book asks whether loyalty is a virtue, when killing is murder, whether noble savagery beats resentful respectability, and whether anarchy among rivals must end, as Hobbes said, nasty, brutish, and short.
188 - The Ultimate South Park and Philos: South Park is Trey Parker and Matt Stone's notoriously foul-mouthed animated satire, running since 1997, in which four Colorado boys skewer fanatics of every stripe, from Scientologists to smug hybrid drivers. The editors argue it is essentially philosophy TV: like Socrates, it corrupts the youth into questioning authority. Essays treat it as a logic textbook of fallacies, a defense of believing only on evidence, and a case that vulgarity breaks through repression.
189 - The Ultimate Star Trek and Philoso: Star Trek is the science-fiction franchise about Starfleet crews exploring the galaxy under utopian ideals and the Prime Directive, spanning shows from Kirk and Picard to Voyager. Philosophy comes built in: thought experiments about personhood for the android Data, duplication and the self, captains' guilt and moral injury, whether Kirk is right to smash contented utopias, and whether Kantian rules or Confucian character should guide encounters with alien cultures.
190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philoso: Star Wars is the landmark space-fantasy film saga about the Jedi, the Force, and the fall and redemption of Darth Vader. Beyond lightsabers it stages serious philosophy: the Jedi as Stoics, the Sith as Nietzschean masters of will, Luke Skywalker as Kierkegaard's knight of faith when he refuses to kill his father, destiny versus free will for the prophesied Anakin, and whether good and evil are, as Palpatine claims, merely points of view.
191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes B: This sequel volume covers Star Wars after Disney's 2012 takeover: the prequels, The Clone Wars, Rogue One, and The Mandalorian, organized chronologically through the saga. The expanded material deepens the philosophy: Qui-Gon Jinn as a Daoist sage, the clone army as Foucault's discipline made flesh, bioethics of Anakin's cybernetic body, Padme through feminist readings, and droid minds and love, all while the saga mirrors today's culture wars over representation.
192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Wou: Superman, DC's flagship superhero since 1938, is the invulnerable alien raised as Clark Kent who chooses restraint and hope. This book runs its essays as a debate over the endless fan question: Batman versus Superman, who is the better hero? Along the way it examines Nietzsche's overman, chivalry, political obligation, evolutionary altruism, and Aristotle's rhetoric, weighing whether the Boy Scout's self-giving or the Dark Knight's grim vigilance better models who we should become.
193 - Supernatural and Philosophy - Meta: Supernatural is the long-running CW series about brothers Sam and Dean Winchester, who crisscross America in a Chevy Impala hunting ghosts, demons, and eventually angels themselves. Its monster-of-the-week format turns out to suit philosophy: when are hunters justified in killing what they hunt, are monsters persons, do the brothers have free will against a scripted destiny, and can Hell's eternal torment ever be a proportionate punishment for a bad deal?
